Community Health Nursing 
Community Health Nursing is a synthesis of nursing knowledge and practice, as well as the science and 
practice of public health, implemented through the systematic use of the nursing process and other

Strategies 
(1)​ Reorientation and reorganization of the national health care system with the establishment of 
functional support mechanism in support of the mandate of devolution under the Local 
Government Code 1991 
(2)​ Effective preparation and enabling process for health action at all levels 
(3)​ Mobilization of the people to know their communities and identifying their basic health needs 
with the end in view of providing appropriate solutions (including legal measures) leading to 
self-reliance and self-determination 
(4)​ Development and utilization of appropriate technology focusing on local indigenous resources 
available in and acceptable to the community 
(5)​ Organization of communities arising from their unexpressed needs which they have decided to 
address and that this is continually evolving in pursuit of their own development 
(6)​ Increase opportunities for community participation in local level planning, management, 
monitoring and evaluation within the context of regional and national objectives 
(7)​ Development of intra-sectoral linkages with other government and private agencies so that 
programs of the health sector is closely linked with those of other socio-economic sectors at the 
national, intermediate and community levels 
(8)​ Emphasizing partnership so that the health workers and the community leaders/members view 
each other as partners rather than merely providers and receiver of health care respectively 
Health Care Delivery System 
-​
the totality of societal services and activities designed to protect or restore the health of 
individuals, families, groups and communities.

(1) public sector which is largely financed through tax-based budgeting system at both 
national and local levels and where health care generally given free at the point of service 
(2) the private sector which is largely market-oriented and where health care is paid 
through user fees at the point of service. 
 
Levels of Health Care 
(1)​ Primary level of care (Accessible) - health care provided by center physicians, PHNs, RH 
midwives, BHWs, traditional healers and others at the barangay health stations (BHS) and RHU. 
The primary health facility is usually the first contact between the community members and the 
other levels of the health facility. Provides basic health care services. 
(2)​ Secondary level of care - usually given in health facilities either privately owned or government 
operated such as infirmaries, municipal and district hospitals and out-patient departments or 
provincial hospitals, It is capable of performing minor surgeries and performing some simple 
laboratory examinations. 
(3)​ Tertiary level of care - rendered by specialists including medical centers as well as regional and 
provincial hospitals and specialized hospitals. Complicated cases and intensive care requires 
tertiary care.

(1)​ Live attenuated vaccine - use live, but weakened pathogens (not safe for pregnant 
women/immunocompromised)

cause allergic reaction

proteins or sugars that trigger immune response

immune response

produce a protein similar to one found to the surface of pathogen

Uterus 
 
Menstrual Hormones 
-​
Estrogen: Produced by the ovaries, estrogen is crucial for developing and thickening the uterine 
lining (endometrium) and plays a role in follicle development.  
-​
Progesterone: Also produced by the ovaries (specifically after ovulation), progesterone maintains 
the uterine lining and prepares the uterus for a potential pregnancy.  
-​
Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH): Released by the pituitary gland, FSH stimulates the 
growth of follicles (which contain eggs) in the ovaries.  
-​
Luteinizing Hormone (LH): Another hormone released by the pituitary gland, LH triggers 
ovulation (the release of an egg from the ovary).  
-​
Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH): Produced by the hypothalamus (a part of the 
brain), GnRH stimulates the pituitary gland to release FSH and LH, initiating the menstrual cycle.  
Phases of Menstruation 
-​
Follicular Phase (1-14): Follicles in the ovaries start to develop, and the uterine lining begins to 
thicken. This phase begins with the end of menstruation and ends with ovulation. (FSH) 
-​
Menstrual - bleeding (day 1-6) decreased estrogen and progesterone 
-​
Proliferative - thickening (day 7-13) increased estrogen and decreased progesterone 
-​
Ovulation: An egg is released from an ovary and travels down the fallopian tube, making it 
available for fertilization. Ovulation typically occurs around day 14 of a 28-day cycle.  
-​
If fertilization has occurred -> after 6-8 days -> implantation (fundus) ->hCG production 
-> maintains corpus luteum for 1st trimester -> production of estrogen and progesterone 
-> to maintain endometrial lining -> amenorrhea -> pregnancy 
-​
Luteal Phase (15-28): After ovulation, the body prepares for a potential pregnancy. If 
fertilization doesn't occur, the uterine lining sheds, and the cycle restarts. This phase is 
characterized by rising progesterone levels. (LH) 
-​
Secretory - twisted and spongy (day 15-26) increased progesterone, decreased estrogen 
-​
Ischemic - vasoconstriction (day 27-28) corpus luteum -> whitish corpus albicans -> no 
estrogen and progesterone production -> menstruation 
-​
Menstruation (Menstrual Phase): This is when the uterine lining (endometrium) sheds, 
resulting in menstrual bleeding. This phase typically lasts 3-7 days

text.127:
Essential Intrapartum and Newborn Care 
-​
a set of evidence-based practices focused on improving newborn care and reducing infant 
mortality. 
-​
Core Principles: 
-​
EINC emphasizes immediate and thorough drying of the newborn, followed by 
skin-to-skin contact with the mother, delayed cord clamping (1-3 minutes after birth), and 
the initiation of breastfeeding without separating the baby from the mother.  
-​
Evidence-Based: 
-​
These practices are supported by research and recommended by organizations like the 
Department of Health (DOH) and the World Health Organization (WHO).  
-​
Impact: 
-​
EINC aims to reduce neonatal mortality rates by ensuring consistent and high-quality care 
for newborns during the critical first moments after birth.  
-​
Implementation: 
-​
The program is designed to be implemented by skilled birth attendants in all settings, 
including both government and private facilities.  
-​
"Unang Yakap": 
-​
EINC is also known as "Unang Yakap" in the Philippines, where it is a key component of 
the Department of Health's efforts to improve maternal and newborn health.  
-​
Four time-bound interventions: 
1.​ Immediate drying 
a.​ Using a clean, dry cloth, thoroughly dry the baby, wiping the face, eyes, head, 
front, back, arms and legs 
2.​ Skin-to-skin contact 
a.​ If a baby is crying and breathing normally, avoid any manipulation such as 
routine suctioning that may cause trauma or introduce infection. Place the 
newborn prone on the mother’s abdomen or chest skin-to-skin 
b.​ Cover the newborn’s back with a blanket and head with a bonnet. Place 
identification band on ankle 
3.​ Proper cord clamping and cutting 
a.​ Clamp and cut the cord after cord pulsations have stopped (1-3 minutes) 
b.​ Put ties tightly around the cord at 2cms and 5cms from the newborn’s abdomen 
c.​ Cut between the ties with sterile instrument 
d.​ Observe for oozing blood 
e.​ Do not milk the cord towards the newborn 
f.​
After cord clamping, ensure oxytocin 10IU IM given to the mother 
4.​ Non-separation of baby from mother & breastfeeding initiation
text.128:
a.​ Observe the newborn. Only when the newborn shows feeding cues (opening 
mouth, tonguing, licking, rooting), make verbal suggestions to the mother to 
encourage her newborn to move toward the breast 
b.​ Counsel on positioning and attachment 
c.​ When the baby is ready, advise the mother to: 
i.​
Make sure the newborn’s neck is neither flexed nor twisted 
ii.​
Make sure the newborn is facing the breast, with the newborn’s nose 
opposite her nipple and chin touching the breast 
iii.​
Hold the newborn’s body close to her body 
iv.​
Support the newborn’s body, not just the neck and shoulder 
v.​
Wait until her newborn’s mouth is opened wide 
vi.​
Move her newborn into her breast, aiming the infant’s lower lip well 
below the nipple 
vii.​
Look for signs of good attachment and suckling: 
1.​ Mouth wide open 
2.​ Lower lip turned outward 
3.​ Baby's chin touching the breast 
4.​ Suckling is slow, deep and some pauses 
5.​ If the attachment or suckling is not good, try again and reassess 
Notes: 
-​
Health workers should not touch the newborn unless there is a medical indication 
-​
Do not give sugar water, formula or other prelacteals 
-​
Do not give bottles or pacifiers 
-​
Do not throw away colostrum

-​
Human intelligence progresses through series of stages based on age, with the child at each

Jean Piaget’s Four Stages of Cognitive Development 
(1)​ Sensorimotor (birth to 2 years old): the child develops a sense of self separate from the 
environment and the concept of object permanence; that is, tangible objects do not cease 
to exist just because they are out of sight. He/she begins to form mental images 
(2)​ Preoperational (2-6 years old): the child develops the ability to express self with 
language, understands the meaning of symbolic gestures, and begins to classify objects 
(3)​ Concrete operational (6-12 years): the child begins to apply logic to thinking, 
understands spatially and reversibility and is increasingly social and able to apply rules; 
however thinking is still concrete 
(4)​ Formal operational (12-15 years old): the child learns to think and reason in abstract 
terms, further develops logical thinking and reasoning, and achieves cognitive maturity

Traction 
-​
Can be short-term or long term 
-​
The exertion of a pulling force applied in two directions to reduce and immobilize fractures 
-​
Goals: 
-​
Realign fracture fragments 
-​
Correct or prevent deformity 
-​
Decrease muscle spasm and pain 
-​
Principles of effective traction 
-​
Whenever traction is applied, countertraction should also be used = provides a force 
acting in the opposite direction (usually the patient’s body weight or bed elevation) 
-​
Traction must be continuous 
-​
Skeletal traction is never interrupted 
-​
Skin traction may be removed for skin care but must be reapplied promptly 
-​
Weights should not be removed unless prescribed 
-​
Good body alignment must be maintained at all times 
-​
Ropes must be unobstructed (move smoothly and not fray) 
-​
Weights must hang freely, never rest on the bed or floor 
-​
Knots in the rope or foot plate must not touch the pukky or foot of the bed (prevents 
interference with traction pull) 
-​
Types of traction: 
-​
Skeletal traction 
-​
Provides continuous traction for fractures of the femur, tibia and cervical spine 
-​
Applied mechanically to the bone using pins, wires or tongs 
-​
Typical weight: 25-40 lbs (11-18 kg) depending on the fracture and patient size 
-​
How: 
-​
Maintain surgical asepsis 
-​
Perform surgical scrub using chlorhexidine solution 
-​
Infiltrate local anesthetic at insertion site and periosteum 
-​
Make a small skin incision -> drill sterile pin or wire through bone 
-​
After insertion, pin, or wire is attached to traction bow or caliper 
-​
Cover ends of pin or wire with protective caps

Inflammatory

-​
First 48 hours: cover site with sterile absorbent non-stick 
dressing and secure with rolled gauze or ace bandage 
-​
After 48-72 hours: perform pin site care daily or weekly 
-​
Clean using chlorhexidine (2 mg/ml) solution; if contraindicated, 
use sterile saline solution

-​

-​

-​
Buck’s ((extension) traction: alleviate muscle spasms and immobilize

-​

freely over edge of bed 
-​
Ensure weight is 2-3.5 (4.5-8 lbs) only 
-​
Elevate foot of bed to provide countertraction 
-​
Russell’s skin (sling) traction: uses sling to raise lower leg and maintain

-​
Pelvic skin traction: relieve low back, hip, or leg pain; reduce muscle

Cast Complications 
Compartment Syndrome 
-​
Medical, painful emergency condition mostly in lower leg 
-​
Pressure increases within one or more compartments, usually in extremities = decreased blood 
flow -> tissue ischemia and neurologic impairment 
-​
Common among young adults; may take up to 48 hours for symptoms to be present 
-​
Neurologic damage may be irreversible if untreated within 4-12 hours 
-​
Assessment (6P’s): 
-​
Pain (severe, unrelieved by opioids, disproportionate) 
-​
Pallor 
-​
Poikilothermia (coolness) 
-​
Paralysis (loss of movement) 
-​
Paresthesia (tingling/numbness) 
-​
Pulselessness (late sign) 
-​
Intervention: 
-​
Univalve or bivalve the cast/dressing 
-​
Fasciotomy (anterolateral or posteromedial removal of fascia) 
-​
Wound left unclosed for 3-5 days 
-​
Cover with moist, sterile saline dressing or aseptic sheet 
-​
Negative-pressure wound therapy (VAC) 
-​
Splint in functional position + elevate + passive ROM 
-​
Once resolved, debride + close with skin graft 
Pressure Ulcer 
-​
Pressure on soft tissues causing anoxia and pressure ulcers 
-​
Typically reports very painful “hot spot” and tightness under cast 
-​
May feel warmth in affected area 
-​
Drainage may stain cast and emit unpleasant odor 
-​
Extensive loss of tissue with skin breakdown and necrosis 
-​
Intervention: 
-​
Windowing - ensure prevention of window edema 
Disuse Syndrome 
-​
Muscle atrophy and loss of strength = deterioration of body system 
-​
Intervention: 
-​
Isometric muscle contraction exercises/muscle setting exercises

Fracture Complications 
Fat Embolism Syndrome 
-​
Movement of fat globules/foreign particles into pulmonary circulation 
-​
Occurs within 24 - 72 hours of injury; mostly in males (10-40 years old) with closed fractures 
-​
Assessment (classic triad): 
-​
Hypoxemia 
-​
Neurologic changes 
-​
Petechial rash (upper body, conjunctiva, oral mucosa) 
-​
Sudden chest pain 
-​
Dyspnea/ difficulty breathing 
-​
Restlessness and confusion 
-​
Coughing with bilateral crackles 
-​
Diagnosis 
-​
Clinical suspicion (triad) + imaging (CXR, CT) 
-​
Intervention (supportive) 
-​
Immobilization of fracture 
-​
Oxygenation (humidified O2) 
-​
IV fluids to maintain perfusion 
-​
IV anticoagulant (heparin) 
-​
Intubation + mechanical ventilation if ABG indicates severe hypoxemia

Disportionate regional pain in limb following fracture, soft tissue injury, or surgery

Hip Fracture 
-​
Risk factors 
-​
Age > 65 years old 
-​
Women (osteoporosis risk) 
-​
Higher risk for falls 
-​
Types: 
-​
Intracapsular - fracture of femoral head and neck 
-​
High risk of vascular damage on neck of femur = ischemia -> avascular necrosis 
-​
Extracapsular - fracture outside joint capsule = base of femoral neck to distal lesser 
trochanter 
-​
Assessment: 
-​
Pain over outer thigh or groin 
-​
Discomfort with hip flexion and rotation 
-​
Shortening, adduction, external rotation 
-​
Diagnosis: X-ray 
-​
Intervention: 
-​
Intracapsular fracture - broken femoral head within joint capsule 
-​
Preoperatively: reduce fracture and decrease spasms with skin traction 
-​
Surgical: hip replacement (hemi/total arthroplasty) or ORIF 
-​
Postoperatively: prevent dislocation 
-​
Avoid hip flexion >90 degrees 
-​
Avoid crossing legs or pointing toes inward 
-​
Ensure correct positioning 
-​
Extracapsular fracture - fracture outside joint capsule 
-​
Preoperatively: reduce pain and spasms with skin traction or balanced suspension 
-​
Surgical: ORIF with nail plate or intramedullary fixation 
-​
Postoperatively: 
-​
Institute safety precautions 
-​
Maintain leg and hip alignment 
-​
Prevent internal or external rotation 
-​
Turn only to unaffected side if needed 
-​
Elevate HOB 30 to 45 degrees

Total Hip Arthroplasty 
-​
Replacement of severely damaged hip with an artificial joint 
-​

Femoral fracture 
-​
Osteoarthritis 
-​
Rheumatoid arthritis 
-​
Avascular necrosis of hips

Maintain femoral head in acetabular cup for approximately 4 months 
-​
Avoid hip full flexion, adduction and internal rotation 
-​

-​
Supine 
-​
Abduction splint = wedge pillow or two pillows between legs 
-​
Continuous boot = prevents leg rotation and prevents pressure ulcer on heels 
-​
Never flex hip >90 degrees 
-​
Movement: turning or bedpan 
-​
Keep operative hip in abduction 
-​
Don’t turn on operative side 
-​
No bending forward

High seat (orthopedic) chairs 
-​
Hips higher (not lower) than knees 
-​
No leg crossing 
-​
Allowed to sit for <1 hour only 
-​
Activity resumptions 
-​
Stair climbing and driving resumes within 3-6 months 
-​
Sexual activity resumes at about 3 months

Assistive Devices 
-​
Crutches 
-​
Principles 
-​
Client 
-​
Distance between axilla and axillary pad on crutch should be 2-3 finger 
widths in axilla 
-​
Elbow should be slightly flexed = 20-30 degrees 
-​
Should look up and outward when ambulating 
-​
Place crutches 6-10 inches diagonally in front of foot 
-​
Stop ambulating if with numbness or tingling in hands or arms 
-​
Nurse 
-​
Stand on affected side when ambulating with client 
-​
Crutch measurement 
-​
If standing: set crutch 5 cm (2 in) below axilla 
-​
If lying down: measure from axillary fold of axilla to sole + 2.5 cm (1 in) 
-​
If using patient’s height: subtract 40 cm (16 in), adjust hand grip to allow 20-30 
degrees elbow flexion 
-​
Crutch gaits 
-​
4-point gait: partial weight bearing both feet; provides maximal support; constant 
shift of weight 
-​
2-point gait: partial weight bearing both feet; provides less support; faster than 
4-point gait 
-​
3-point gait: non-weight bearing; requires good balance and arm strength; faster 
gait 
-​
Swing-to-gait: for partial weight bearing limitations with bilateral lower 
extremities prostheses 
-​
Swing-through gait: requires adequate muscle power and balance in arms and 
legs 
-​
Crutch movement 
-​
Sitting and standing 
-​
Place unaffected leg against front of the chair 
-​
Move crutches at unaffected side 
-​
Grasp arm of chair with hand of affected side 
-​
Flex knee of unaffected leg to lower self into chair while placing affected 
leg straight out in front 
-​
Going up stairs “Up with the GOOD” (move unaffected leg first) 
-​
Going down stairs “Down with the BAD” (move affected leg first) 
-​
Canes 
-​
Principles
text.243:

-​
Handle at greater trochanter level 
-​
Elbow flexed at 20-30 degrees

Hold cane 6-10 inches to side of foot 
-​
Hold cane in hand of unaffected side 
-​
Move cane together with affected leg 
-​
Inspect rubber tips regularly 
-​
Walkers 
-​
Principles 
-​
Stand adjacent on affected side 
-​
Pull all four points flat on floor 
-​
Move walker first 
-​
Then affected/weaker foot 
-​
Then unaffected/stronger foot 
Musculoskeletal Disorders 
Upper Extremity Disorder 
1.​ Bursitis and tendonitis 
a.​ Bursitis: inflammation of bursae 
b.​ Tendonitis: inflammation of muscle tendon sheaths with repetitive stretching 
c.​ Intervention 
i.​
Self-limiting + pain relief 
1.​ Conservation treatment = rest + intermittent ice and heat to joint + 
NSAIDs 
2.​ Corticosteroid injection 
3.​ Anthroscopic surgery if shoulder pain and weakness persist 
2.​ Loose bodies (joint mice) 
a.​ Occurs in joint spaces as result of articular cartilage wear and bone erosion 
b.​ Fragments interfere with joint movement 
c.​ Intervention 
i.​
Anthroscopic surgery if fragments cause pain or mobiility issues 
3.​ Impingement syndrome 
a.​ General term for impaired movement of rotator cuff of shoulder 
b.​ Occurs from repetitive overhead movement of arm or acute trauma 
c.​ Results in rotator cuff tendons or subacromial bursa grinding against coracoacromial arch 
d.​ Assessment 
i.​
Early

4.​ Carpal Tunnel Syndrome 
a.​ Entrapment neuropathy when median nerve is compressed by thickened flexor tendon

Lower Extremity Disorder 
1.​ Corn 
a.​ Area of hyperkeratosis by internal pressure 
b.​ 5th toe most commonly involved 
c.​ Interventions 
i.​
Podiatrist: soak and scrape horny layer

Protective shiled/pad + separation by lamb’s wool or gauze

2.​ Hallux valgus (bunion) 
a.​ Great toe deviates laterally due to marked prominence of medial aspect of first 
metatarsophangeal joint 
b.​ Osseous enlargement (exostosis) of medial site -> bursitis 
c.​ Intervention 
i.​
Shoe that conforms to foot shape 
ii.​
Corticosteroid injection (for acute inflammation) 
iii.​
Surgical excision of exostosis + toe realignment 
3.​ Hammer toe 
a.​ Flexion deformity of interphangeal joint 
b.​ Toes pulled upward while metatarsophangeal joints forced down 
c.​ Corns = top, callus = underneath 
d.​ Intervention

Respiratory System 
Anatomy 
-​
comprised of the upper and lower airway structures, responsible for ventilation 
-​

-​

and humidifies and warms the air as it is inhaled 
-​

in speech 
-​

larynx 
-​

and the trachea 
-​
Lower respiratory system - enables the exchange of gases to regulate serum PaO2, PaCO2 and 
pH 
-​
Trachea (windpipe) - serves as the passage between larynx and bronchi 
-​
Lungs - paired elastic structures enclosed in the thoracic cage, which is an airtight 
chamber with distensible walls 
-​

-​

text.254:
-​
Alveolar stretch receptors respond to inspiration by sending signals to 
inhibit inspiratory neurons in the brain stem to prevent lung over 
distention 
-​
During expiration stretch receptors stop sending signals to inspiratory 
neurons and inspiratory is ready to start again 
-​
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged across the alveolar capillary 
membrane by process of diffusion 
-​
Neural control of respiration is located in the medulla. The respiratory 
center in the medulla is stimulated by the concentration of carbon dioxide 
in the blood 
-​
Chemoreceptors, a secondary feedback system, located in the carotid 
arteries and aortic arch respond to hypoxemia. These chemoreceptors 
stimulate the medulla

from the blood stream to the lungs. Occurs in the alveoli through passive diffusion 
-​

infarction, cardiogenic shock 
-​
Low ventilation-high perfusion ratio - client with pneumonia, atelectasis, mucus plug, 
tumor, COPD 
-​
Low ventilation-low perfusion ratio - silent, pneumothorax, ARDS

Inflammation of the lung parenchyma caused by various microorganisms, including bacteria,

-​
Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease that primarily affects the lung parenchyma 
-​
It is also transmitted to other parts of the body, including meninges, kidneys, bones and lymph 
nodes 
-​
The primary infectious agent, M. tuberculosis is an acid fast aerobic rod that grows slowly and 
sensitive to heat and ultraviolet light spreads from person to person by airborne transmission 
-​

-​

-​
Data from the history, physical examination, TB test, CXR, and microbiologic studies are 
used to classify TB into one of five classes 
-​
A classification scheme provides public health officials with a systematic way to monitor 
epidemiology and treatment of the disease 
-​

-​
Class 1: exposure; no evidence of infection 
-​
Class 2: latent infection; no disease 
-​
Class 3: disease; clinically active

pyrazinamide and ethambutol and is administered daily for 8 weeks

additional 4-7 months

INH-associated peripheral neuropathy

Surgical Classification 
According to Magnitude 
-​
Major procedure 
-​
High risk for morbidity and mortality

Extensive or prolonged 
-​
Large amount of blood loss 
-​

-​
Minor procedure: procedures that are not included in the characteristics of major procedures

According to Purpose 
-​
Diagnostic: to establish the disease or condition (biopsy) 
-​
Exploratory: to determine cause of unexplained symptoms; to determine the extent of a 
condition (exploratory laparotomy) 
-​
Preventive/Prophylactic: stops the development of a disease (removal of pre-cancerous lesions) 
-​
Curative 
-​
Ablative: removal of body part 
-​
Constructive: repair for congenital defects 
-​
Reconstructive or cosmetics: repair of a damaged or diseased organs (mammoplasty or 
facelift) 
-​
Palliative: to reduce distressful signs and symptoms 
According to the Degree of Urgency 
-​
Optional: surgery is scheduled completely at the preference of the patient 
-​
Elective: the approximate time for surgery is at the convenience of the patient; failure to have 
surgery is not catastrophic 
-​
Required: the condition requires surgery within a few weeks 
-​
Urgent: the surgical problem requires attention within 24 to 48 hours 
-​
Emergency: the situation requires immediate surgical attention without delay 
According to Invasiveness 
-​
Open surgery: requires cutting of skin and tissues for a full view of the organs or structures 
involved 
-​
Minimally invasive surgery: does not require large incision (keyhole surgery/laparoscopy 
surgery) 
Informed Consent 
Informed consent: the patient’s autonomous decision about whether to undergo a surgical procedure. It is 
the process of informing the patient about the surgical procedure; that is risks and possible complications 
of surgery and anesthesia 
-​

Post-Operative Phase 
Care of Patient in the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU)  
-​
Phases of post-anesthesia care 
-​
Phase I: care of surgical patients immediately after surgery and for the patient whose 
condition warrants close monitoring and intensive care is provided 
-​
Phase II: surgical patient’s condition no longer requires close monitoring provided in 
phase I PACU. Patient is prepared for self-care or care in the hospital or extended care 
setting 
-​
Phase III: setting in which the patient is cared for immediate postoperative period and 
then prepared for discharge from the facility 
-​
Determining readiness for discharge from the PACU 
-​
many hospitals use a scoring system (Aldrete score) to determine the patient’s general 
condition and readiness for transfer from the PACU 
-​
Throughout the recovery period, the patient’s physical signs are observed and evaluated 
by means of a scoring system based on the set of objective criteria 
-​
The patient is assessed at regular intervals and a total score is calculated and recorded 
-​
Aldrete score is usually 8-10 before discharge from the PACU, the patient with the score 
of <7 must remain in the PACU until condition improves or they transferred to ICU 
-​
Areas of assessment in Adrete score includes: 
-​
Activity 
-​
Respiration 
-​
circulation 
-​
Consciousness 
-​
oxygen saturation 
-​
Priority #1: restoration of homeostasis and prevent complications 
-​
Priority #2: maintain and promote adequate airway and respiratory function 
-​
Priority #3: maintain adequate cardiac function and promote tissue perfusion 
-​
Priority #4: maintain adequate fluid and electrolyte balance and adequate renal function  
-​
Sufficient fluids to maintain extracellular fluids and blood volume 
-​
Prevent fluid overload with resultant 
-​
pulmonary congestion and edema

Upper GI series 
-​
Delineates the entire GI tract after the introduction of contrast agent (Barium swallow) 
-​
Enables the examiner to detect or exclude anatomic or functional derangement of the 
upper GI organs or sphincters 
-​

syndromes 
-​
Nursing interventions: 
-​
Clear liquid diet with NPO from midnight the night before the study 
-​
Smoking, chewing gum and mints can stimulate gastric motility so the nurse 
advises against these practices 
-​
Increase fluid intake to facilitate evacuation of stool and the radiopaque liquid 
-​
Typically, oral medications are withheld on the morning of the study and resumed 
that evening but each patient’s medication regimen is evaluated on an individual 
basis 
-​
Lower GI series 
-​
Visualization of the lower GI tract 
-​
with introduction of barium enema 
-​

images are obtained

-​

-​
Low residue diet 1-2 days before the test 
-​
clear liquid diet, NPO after midnight; and cleansing enemas until returns to clear 
the following morning 
-​
Laxative is given before and after the procedure 
-​
Increased fluid intake after the procedure 
-​
Evaluation of bowel movement for evacuation of barium 
-​
Esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD) 
-​
Direct visualization of esophageal, gastric and duodenal mucosa through a lighted 
endoscope 
-​
After the patient is sedated, the endoscope is lubricated with a water-soluble lubricant and 
passed smoothly and slowly along the back of the mouth and down into the esophagus
text.418:
-​
The procedure usually takes about 30 minutes 
-​

-​
Use of topical anesthetic agents and moderate sedation makes it important to monitor and 
maintain the patient’s oral airway during and after the procedure 
-​
Precautions must be taken to protect the scope, because the fiberoptic bundles can be 
broken if the scope is bent at an acute angle 
-​
Nursing interventions: 
-​
The patient should be NPO for 8 hours prior to the examination 
-​
before the introduction of the endoscope, the patient is given a local anesthetic 
gargle or spray 
-​
Midazolam (Versed) a sedative that provides moderate sedation and relieves 
anxiety during the procedure 
-​
Atropine may be administered to reduce secretions and glucagon may be 
administered to relax smooth muscle  
-​
The patient is positioned left lateral position to facilitate clearance of pulmonary 
secretions and provide smooth entry of the scope 
-​
After gastroscopy, assessment includes LOC, VS, oxygen saturation, pain level 
-​
Monitor signs of perforation such as pain, bleeding, unusual difficulty of 
swallowing, rapidly elevated temperature 
-​
After the patient’s gag reflex has returned, lozenges, saline gargle and oral 
analgesics agents may be offered to relieve minor throat discomfort 
-​
Patients who were sedated for the procedure must remain in bed until fully alert

-​
Visualization of the common bile duct, the pancreatic, hepatic duct, through the ampulla

-​

Direct visual inspection of the large intestine 
-​

snare and cautery through the colonoscope

Direct visualization of the organs and structures within the abdomen, permitting 
visualization and identification of an growths, anomalies and inflammatory processes 
-​
A pneumoperitoneum (injecting carbon dioxide into the peritoneal cavity to separate the 
intestines from the pelvic organs) is created 
-​

-​
Laparoscopy usually requires general anesthesia and sometimes requires that the stomach

Psychiatric Nursing 
-​
Specialized field within nursing focused on the care of individuals with mental health disorders 
and substance abuse issues 
Mental Health 
-​
State of emotional, psychological, and social wellness as evidenced by satisfying interpersonal 
relationships, effective behavior and coping, positive self-concept and emotional stability 
Factors affecting Mental Health 
(1)​ Individual/Personal factor - person’s biological make up, autonomy, and independence, 
self-esteem, capacity for growth, vitality, ability to find meaning in life, emotional resilience or 
hardiness, sense of belonging, reality orientation, and coping or stress management abilities 
(2)​ Interpersonal/relationship factor - include effective communication , ability to help others, 
intimacy, and balance of separateness and connectedness
text.446:
(3)​ Social/cultural/environmental factor - include a sense of community, access to adequate 
resources, intolerance of violence, support of diversity among people, mastery of the environment 
and a positive yet realistic view of one’s world 
Mental Illness 
-​
Includes disorders that affect mood, behavior, and thinking such as depression, schizophrenia, 
anxiety disorders and addictive disorders 
-​
Causes significant distress, impaired functioning, or both 
 
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition (DSM-5) 
-​
A taxonomy published by the American Psychiatric Association 
-​
Describes all mental disorders, outlining specific diagnostic criteria for each based on clinical 
experience and research 
-​
Three purposes: 
-​
To provide a standardized nomenclature and language for all mental health professionals 
-​
To present defining characteristics or symptoms that differentiate specific diagnoses 
-​
To assist in identifying the underlying causes of disorders

-​

Establish a therapeutic nurse-client relationship

Facilitate the client’s expression of emotions

Teach the client and family necessary self-care skills 
-​
Recognize the client’s needs 
-​
Implement intervention designed to address the client’s needs

Guide the client toward identifying a plan of action to a satisfying and socially accepted 
resolution

Crisis 
-​
A turning point in an individual’s life that produces an overwhelming emotional response, when 
coping mechanism fails 
-​
Duration: 4-6 weeks (self-limiting) 
-​
Focus: Gestalt therapy (focuses on the here and the now) 
-​
Goal: to help patient return to pre-crisis level 
-​
Stages of Crisis: 
-​
The person is exposed to a stressor, experiences anxiety and tries to cope in a customary 
fashion 
-​
Anxiety increases when customary coping skills is ineffective 
-​
The person makes all possible efforts to deal with the stressor including attempts at new 
methods of coping 
-​
When coping attempts fail, the person experiences disequilibrium and significant distress 
-​
Three categories: 
-​
Maturational/developmental crisis: predictable events in the normal course of life such 
as leaving home for the first time, getting married, having a baby, and beginning a career 
-​
Situational crisis: unanticipated or sudden events that threaten the individual’s integrity 
such as the death of a loved one, loss of job, physical or emotional illness of a family 
member 
-​
Adventitious/social crisis: include natural disasters like floods, earthquakes or 
hurricanes, war, terrorist attacks, riots and violent crimes such as rape or murder 
-​
Crisis Intervention - includes a variety of techniques based on the assessment of the individual 
(1)​ Directive intervention: designed to assess the person’s health status and promote 
problem-solving, such as offering the person new information, knowledge, or mean; 
raising the suggestions or courses of action

Staffing Formula 
1.​ Categorize according to the level of care needed. Multiply the total number of patients by the 
percentage of patients at each level of care 
2.​ Find the total number of nursing care hours needed by the patients at each category level 
a.​ Find the number of patients at each level by the average number of nursing care hours 
needed per day 
b.​ Get the sum of the nursing care hours needed at the various levels 
3.​ Find the actual number of nursing care hours needed by the given number of patients. Multiply 
the total nursing care hours needed per day by the total number of days in a year 
4.​ Find the actual number of nursing care hours rendered by each nursing personnel per year 
a.​ Multiply the number of hours on duty per day by the actual working days per year 
5.​ Find the total number of nursing personnel needed 
a.​ Divide the total number of nursing of nursing care needed per year by the actual number 
of working hours rendered by an employee per year 
b.​ Find the number of relievers. Multiply the number of nursing personnel needed by 0.15 
(40 hours per week) or by 0.12 (48 hours per week) 
c.​ Add the number of relievers to the number of personnel need 
6.​ Categorize the nursing personnel into professional and non-professionals. Multiply the number of 
personnel according to the ratio of professionals to non-professionals 
7.​ Distribute by shifts

-​
Paternalism: means overriding a person’s choices or actions for their own good, usually 
with the intention of protecting them from harm or promoting their well-being. 
-​
Informed consent:  
-​
A voluntary agreement by a patient to undergo a medical procedure, treatment, or 
participation in research, after being fully informed of all relevant facts. 
-​
It respects the ethical principle of autonomy (the patient’s right to decide). 
-​
Essential Elements: 
-​
Disclosure – The patient must receive complete, accurate, and 
understandable information (nature of the procedure, risks, benefits, 
alternatives, and consequences of refusal). 
-​
Comprehension – The patient must understand the information 
provided. 
-​
Voluntariness – The decision must be made freely, without coercion or 
undue influence. 
-​
Competence – The patient must have the capacity (legal age, sound 
mind) to make decisions. 
-​
Consent – Expressed either verbally or in writing (usually written for 
major procedures) 
-​
Types 
-​
Implied consent: Assumed through actions (e.g., rolling up a sleeve for 
an injection). 
-​
Expressed consent: Clearly given, verbally or in writing. 
-​
Written Consent: A formal, signed document granting permission for 
specific medical/surgical procedures or research participation. 
-​
Oral Consent: Patient verbally agrees after being fully informed. 
-​
Proxy Consent (Substituted Consent):  Given by a legal guardian, 
parent, or authorized representative when the patient is a minor, 
unconscious, or mentally incapacitated. 
-​
Informed Refusal: When a patient, after being fully informed, refuses 
treatment. 
-​
Nursing Role 
-​
Ensure the patient received accurate information from the physician. 
-​
Clarify any questions or misunderstandings. 
-​
Verify that consent is signed before procedures 
-​
Advocate for the patient if they feel pressured or misinformed 
-​
Veracity 
-​
Truth telling or honesty 
-​
Benevolent deception: The act of withholding the truth or giving incomplete information 
to a patient with the intention of sparing them from distress, anxiety, or harm

Geriatric Nursing 
Geriatric Nursing or Gerontological Nursing is a specialized field focused on providing comprehensive 
care for older adults (typically 60+) to promote their health, independence and quality of life 
Theories of Aging 
Biological Theories 
Aging - decreased cell division -> decreased growth; answers “Why” 
1.​ Gene theory - biological timeline 
2.​ Immunologic theory - decreased immune -> risk of disease -> cell damage -> decreased cell 
division 
3.​ Neuroendocrine/Endocrine theory - decreased in brain function (hypothalamus -> pituitary 
gland) -> decreased hormone T3/T4 -> decreased metabolism 
4.​ Wear and tear theory - the more you use your body, the quicker you die
text.578:
5.​ Free-radical theory - unstable molecules -> cell damage 
6.​ Cross-linkage theory - the manifestation of aging, tight binding of protein (muscle stiffness) -> 
decreased elasticity 
Psychological Theories 
Answers the question “how” 
1.​ Disengagement theory - isolated from society -> agesism 
2.​ Activity theory - increased productivity 
3.​ Continuity theory - maintains values, habit, and behavior 
4.​ Erikson’s psychosocial theory - ego integrity (death is okay) -> satisfaction vs. despair (regrets) 
Aging Changes 
Physiologic Changes 
General rule: decreased physiologic function, increased risk to disease

Positions 
 
1.​ Supine  
a.​ the most natural “at rest” position 
b.​ patient is flat on his back 
c.​ Indication: used in surgery for abdominal, facial and extremity procedures 
2.​ Prone 
a.​ patient will be lying on their stomach 
b.​ Patient lies face down, head is turned to one side 
c.​ indication: drainage of the mouth after oral or neck surgery. It also allows for full 
extension of the knees and legs 
3.​ Lithotomy 
a.​ Common in OB/GYN whether during an exam or labor 
b.​ patient is lying on their back with knees elevated and hips level, often supported by 
stirrups 
c.​ Indication: gynecological procedures and childbirth 
4.​ Sim’s position 
a.​ prone + lateral position 
b.​ The patient lies on his side with his upper leg flexed and drawn in towards the chest and 
the upper arm flexed at the elbow 
c.​ Indication: administering enemas, perineal examination and comfort in pregnancy, may 
be used for colonoscopies 
5.​ Lateral 
a.​ lying on either side 
b.​ Right lateral means the right side of the patient is touching the bed; left lateral means the 
left side of the patient is touching the bed 
c.​ Indications: GI issues and rectal surgery/colonoscopies 
6.​ Fowler’s position 
a.​ Semi fowlers - 30-40; high fowlers - 90 degrees 
b.​ A position which the head and trunk are raised 40-90 degrees 
c.​ Indications: cardiac issues, SOB related to respiratory/cardiac issues, NG placement, 
EGD 
7.​ Trendelenburg 
a.​ “Upside down” or shock position
text.633:
b.​ The position involves a patient lying supine, lowering the head of the bed and raising the 
foot 
c.​ Indication: treat hypotension, during gynecological and abdominal hernia surgeries, 
placement of central lines 
8.​ Reverse trendelenburg 
a.​ Patient is in the supine position with the head of the bed elevated and the foot of the bed 
down 
b.​ Indication: used in surgery to help promote perfusion in obese patients, helpful in treating 
venous air embolism and preventing pulmonary aspiration
